lessons.title: লাল (lal) — "red," a gemstone's name first
lessons.gloss: red — a jeweler's word before it was a color word, and the identical Persian loan Hindi already teaches

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: A new small set of words: not people, not verbs, not places, but the colors of the things around you — starting with the one Bengali did not invent for itself.
লাল (lal) — lāl — red.
লাল (lal) চা (lāl chā) — "red tea," the everyday way to ask for tea without milk.
লাল (lal) is ল (lô) with the vowel sign া (ā), plus a second ল (l, silent at the end): lāl, one long vowel between two of the same consonant.

লাল (lal) is a Persian loan, from Persian la'l, which named one specific thing first: a deep-red gemstone, a ruby or a spinel. Only later did the gem's name widen into the ordinary word for the color itself. Bengali did not build this word out of its own materials, and it did not borrow it alone — Hindi's own word for red is this identical Persian loan, carried into both languages by the same jewelers' trade routes rather than independently invented twice.

segments.instruction: what it named first — "a ruby, not a color"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what it named first — "a ruby, not a color"]

segments.text: What did লাল (lal) originally name, before it meant "red"? (A deep red gemstone.) Did Bengali and Hindi each invent this word separately? (No — both borrowed the identical Persian loan.) One more reach: give the polite excuse-me again, and its softening tense. (মাফ করবেন — the future, "you will do.")

lessons.title: নীল (nil) — "blue," and a word that only looks like "indigo"
lessons.gloss: blue — Sanskrit's word for indigo, one form for every noun it describes

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: The last color was foreign, borrowed whole. This one is Sanskrit's own — and it comes with a famous false friend worth clearing up honestly.
নীল (nil) — nīl — blue.
নীল (nil) জল (nīl jôl) — blue water.
নীল (nil) is ন (nô) with the vowel sign ী (a long ī, the same sound as the short ি but held longer), plus ল (l, silent at the end): nīl.

নীল (nil) is Sanskrit নীল (nil) (nīla), "dark blue" — also the name of the indigo plant and the dye made from it, the same root Hindi's own nīlā carries. One difference is worth stating plainly: Hindi's nīlā changes shape, nīlā/nīlī, for the noun it describes; নীল (nil) never does, one form whether the water, the sky, or the dress is blue.

Here is the honest, careful version of a famous connection. English "indigo" does not come from nīla by sound change. It comes from Greek indikón, simply "the Indian [thing]" — because Greek and Roman traders imported the dye from India and named it for its source. Nīla and "indigo" are not the same word wearing two disguises; they are two separate words for the same dye, linked by the history of trade, not by descent from a shared root.

segments.instruction: one form, always — "nīl," never nīlā or nīlī
segments.source: [YOU SAY: one form, always — "nīl," never *nīlā* or *nīlī*]

segments.text: Does নীল (nil) change shape for the noun it describes, the way Hindi's nīlā does? (No — one form, always.) Does English "indigo" come directly from নীল (nil)/nīla? (No — it is Greek indikón, "the Indian thing"; the two words are linked by trade, not by sound change.) Give "welcome" once more. (স্বাগতম.)

lessons.title: কালো (kalo) — "black," the same word as "time"
lessons.gloss: black — the same word Sanskrit uses for time, and for death

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Blue carried a false friend. This color hides something bigger inside it: the very word Sanskrit uses for time itself, and for death.
কালো (kalo) — kālo — black.
কালো (kalo) চা (kālo chā) — black tea.
কালো (kalo) is ক (kô) with the vowel sign া (ā), plus ল (l) with the vowel sign ো (o): kā-lo.

কালো (kalo) is built on Sanskrit কাল (kāla), a word that covers both "black, dark" and "time." Sanskrit's own tradition ties the two together poetically — time devours everything, and that devouring is imagined as dark — and the same word names the fierce goddess Kālī ("the black/dark one") and stands as an epithet of Yama, the god of death. Hindi's own kālā carries the identical root and the identical story. Be honest, though: whether "black" and "time" are truly one and the same root, or two separate ancient words that poetry and theology later fused into a single idea, is a real, still-debated question among linguists — the cultural connection is certain; the precise etymology underneath it is not.

segments.instruction: what else কাল means — "time," and by extension, death
segments.source: [YOU SAY: what else কাল means — "time," and by extension, death]

segments.text: What does কালো (kalo)'s root, কাল, also mean, besides "black"? (Time — and by extension, death; the same word names the goddess Kālī and Yama's epithet Kāla.) Is it settled that "black" and "time" are the same root? (No — the cultural link is real and ancient, but linguists still debate whether it is one true root or two words later fused.)

lessons.title: সাদা (shada) — "white," the color where the cousins part ways
lessons.gloss: white — a tadbhava worn down from Sanskrit, and the one color where Bengali and Hindi genuinely parted ways

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Every color so far has matched Hindi's, word for word. This one does not — and it is the more interesting choice for it.
সাদা (shada) — shādā — white.
সাদা (shada) দুধ (shādā dudh) — white milk.
সাদা (shada) is স (sô, carrying its familiar tilt to sh) with the vowel sign া (ā), plus দ (dô) with the vowel sign া (ā) again: shā-dā.

সাদা (shada) is usually traced to Sanskrit শ্বেত (śveta), "white," worn down through Middle Bengali into today's everyday word — a tadbhava, the same road মুখ's own twin travelled, only in reverse: here the tadbhava is the common word and the tatsama, শ্বেত (śveto), survives kept whole inside compounds, like শ্বেতাঙ্গ (śvetāngo), "pale-skinned."

This is the one color where Bengali and Hindi genuinely part ways. Every other color word met so far — the borrowed gem-name, the indigo plant, the time-word — Bengali and Hindi share outright. For white, Hindi replaced its own Sanskrit-derived word with a Persian loan, safed. Bengali did not: it kept the native word as its everyday one, and the Persian loan never took hold here the way it did next door.

Is সাদা (shada) a tatsama, kept whole, or a tadbhava, worn down by sound change? (A tadbhava — its tatsama twin, শ্বেত, survives only in compounds, the same split মুখ's own twin showed.) Of the colors met so far, which one did Hindi replace with a Persian loan while Bengali kept the native word? (White — Hindi's safed against Bengali's সাদা (shada).)

lessons.title: সবুজ (shobuj) — "green," and five colors, counted up
lessons.gloss: green — a second Persian loan, and the chapter's payoff on all five colors

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: One color left, and it is a second loan from the same language that gave লাল (lal) its gem — but this time the loan travelled somewhere you already have a word for.
সবুজ (shobuj) — shôbuj — green.
সবুজ (shobuj) চা (shôbuj chā) — green tea.
সবুজ (shobuj) is স (sô, tilted to sh, keeping its own inherent vowel since nothing joins it) plus ব (bô) with the vowel sign ু (u), plus জ (j, silent at the end): shô-bu-j.

সবুজ (shobuj) is borrowed from Persian sabz, "green" — the very same Persian word that gave Hindi and Urdu their word for "vegetable," sabzī, literally "the green things." লাল (lal)'s own Persian gem-name arrived by the same route, from the same trading world, into a different corner of the vocabulary.

Step back and count the five colors this small set has taught: two Persian loans (লাল (lal), সবুজ (shobuj)), two Sanskrit words kept recognizably close to their root (নীল (nil), কালো (kalo)), and one worn down by sound change (সাদা (shada)). A more even split between inherited and borrowed than the food words or the family words showed — color, it turns out, came into Bengali from everywhere at once.

segments.instruction: all five colors — "lāl, nīl, kālo, shādā, shôbuj"

segments.instruction: the two Persian loans, then the two Sanskrit words, then the one worn down — "lāl, shôbuj … nīl, kālo … shādā"

segments.text: What Persian word gives both সবুজ (shobuj) and Hindi's word for "vegetable"? (sabz, "green" — Hindi's sabzī is literally "the green things.") Of the five colors, how many are Persian loans, how many are Sanskrit words, and how many are worn down by sound change? (Two, two, and one — লাল (lal) and সবুজ (shobuj); নীল (nil) and কালো (kalo); সাদা (shada).) Name all five colors, in order. (লাল (lal), নীল (nil), কালো (kalo), সাদা (shada), সবুজ (shobuj).)
